I don't... I don't really know if something is forcing me, exactly. It's hard to explain, because it's not like a person standing there holding a gun to my head, you know? And the boxes... man, the boxes are the worst part. When I'm looking at a pallet, and I have all these cartons of, I don't know, let's say it's automotive parts, right? Heavy stuff. Brake pads, rotors, whatever. I'm supposed to just stack them interlocking so the pallet is stable when they wrap it in plastic. That's what they taught us in the safety course. I just don't know where it comes from. So, no, I wouldn't say something is forcing me, I just... I just honestly don't know.

I mean... I don't really know? It's not like... it's not like when you're holding your breath and your lungs start burning and you just absolutely *have* to gasp for air, you know? It’s nothing like that. 

Like, I can tell you about what happened last Tuesday, right before they actually pulled me off the floor and put me on leave. I was over by the loading dock, Bay 4. The big corrugated metal doors were rolled all the way up, and the wind was blowing in, kind of cold, smelling like diesel exhaust from the trucks. I was working with these smaller cartons—spark plugs, I think, hundreds of them in these little rectangular white and red boxes. And I was putting them in this alternating grid pattern on the concrete, red side up, then white side up, making this massive checkerboard right in the middle of the loading zone. 

And my supervisor, Mike—he's this older guy, been there forever, always walking around carrying this massive insulated silver coffee mug—he came over and he just completely kicked the boxes out of the way. Just booted them right across the floor. And he grabbed me by the shoulder of my safety vest and shook me, just yelling over the noise, "What are you doing, snap out of it, we have trucks waiting!" 

And... I didn't feel angry. I didn't feel like I was gonna explode or panic because I couldn't finish the checkerboard. I didn't feel anxious at all. I just sort of... stopped. I just stood there looking at the spark plug boxes scattered everywhere across the dirty concrete. People always assume you'd get mad or freak out if someone ruins something you're focused on, but no. I just don't really feel anything about it. The pattern was just happening, and then it wasn't. 

I was just standing there while Mike kept yelling, his face getting all red, spit literally flying out of his mouth and catching in the light from the bay doors, and a forklift started backing up behind him... and I just started copying the beeps again right to his face. Not because I was upset that he broke my pattern or because I was trying to make him mad, but just because the machine was beeping and it just happened again. So, yeah, I don't know. I don't really have a feeling about not being able to do it. It's just... nothing, really. I just stand there.

Anxious? No... I mean, I think I just said this, but I don't really think about them at all when I'm not actively doing them. So if I'm not thinking about the patterns, I'm definitely not sitting around worrying about whether or not I'll be allowed to do them.

Relief? Or, like, satisfaction? No. No, man, not at all. 

Like, I know what satisfaction feels like, right? Back when I was taking that supply chain class I told you about, when I finally finished this massive ten-page paper on freight logistics and I hit submit on the computer at, like, 11:59 PM right before the midnight deadline... that was relief. You feel like you actually accomplished something real. 

But the boxes? Or the forklift beeps? It's nothing like that. There's no... payoff. I mean... I don't really know if "must" is the right word. It's not like I feel this intense pressure building up inside me, pushing me to do it, you know? When I'm at home, sitting on the couch in my apartment, watching TV or whatever, I'm not sitting there thinking about the spark plug boxes or the forklift beeps. It's not like a song stuck in my head. I'm not planning out the next pattern I'm going to make on the loading dock. It's really only when I'm right there, in the middle of it all, with the noise and the machines and the concrete floor. \n\nBut, you know, I guess that's exactly why they made me come see you. It's not something I think about beforehand, or after. It just happens when I'm there, and they couldn't handle it anymore, so here I am. But no, I don't sit around thinking about it when I'm off the clock. It's just... it just happens right in the moment.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel anxious when you think about not being able to do one of your patterns or sounds?\n\nPatient: Anxious? No... I mean, I think I just said this, but I don't really think about them at all when I'm not actively doing them. So if I'm not thinking about the patterns, I'm definitely not sitting around worrying about whether or not I'll be allowed to do them. \n\nIt's not like... okay, you know when you have a big test coming up? Like back when I was taking a few classes at the community college, right before I dropped out and got hired at the warehouse. I remember taking this intro to supply chain management class, and the night before the midterm I was just sweating, lying in bed staring at the ceiling fan in my apartment, listening to the motor humming and clicking, totally anxious because I was thinking about failing and wasting my tuition money. That's anxiety. You're anticipating something bad happening. You're dreading a future event. \n\nBut with the boxes or the forklift noises... there's no anticipation like that. I don't sit in my Honda out in the employee parking lot before my shift, gripping the steering wheel, stressing out that Mike is gonna come over and kick my freight around and stop me from making a checkerboard. I don't worry about it. I just walk in, punch my timecard, put on my yellow safety vest, walk out to the loading dock, and... if it happens, it happens. If the forklift backs up, I make the noise. If they stop me, I just stand there. So, no, no anxiety. I don't even have the thought in my head to get anxious about in the first place, you know? It's just not something I worry about.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel any sense of relief or satisfaction when you're able to complete one of your patterns or finish making a sound?\n\nPatient: Relief? Or, like, satisfaction? No. No, man, not at all. \n\nLike, I know what satisfaction feels like, right? Back when I was taking that supply chain class I told you about, when I finally finished this massive ten-page paper on freight logistics and I hit submit on the computer at, like, 11:59 PM right before the midnight deadline... that was relief. I leaned back in my chair, cracked my knuckles, and felt genuinely satisfied. Or even at the warehouse, you know, when we finish unloading a full fifty-three-foot trailer of heavy car parts, and the very last pallet is off the truck, and we just stand by the open bay doors feeling the breeze coming in from the yard... you wipe the sweat off your forehead, maybe take a drink from your water bottle, and you feel good. It just is.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you must perform these patterns or sounds, or is it just something you do?\n\nPatient: I mean... I don't really know if \"must\" is the right word. It's not like that. \n\nBut at the same time, it's not exactly a choice, either. It's not like I'm standing by the conveyor belt, looking at a pallet of spark plug boxes, and I think to myself, \"Hmm, I think I'll arrange these into a nice little checkerboard pattern right now instead of loading them onto the truck.\" I don't decide to do it. It's more like... I'm just doing it. \n\nLike yesterday, before Mike finally lost it and sent me here. The orange Toyota forklift—the one with the squeaky left rear wheel, not the newer one—started backing up near Bay 4. The spotter, Dave, was doing the hand signals, waving his arms to guide the driver back. And suddenly, I was just... frozen. My arms were up in the exact same position as Dave's, and I was making the exact pitch of the reversing alarm. Beep. Beep. Beep. I didn't think, \"Oh, I must do this right now.\" I didn't feel a need to do it. I just... became part of it, I guess? Like I was just another piece of the machinery in the warehouse. \n\nAnd then Mike came over, yelling, face all red like a tomato, screaming at me to snap out of it and move the freight. And I heard him, I really did, but I just kept doing it until the forklift stopped backing up. Control? I mean... no, not really. Look, I feel like I keep saying the exact same thing over and over again to you, but... well, I guess they brought me in here to this clinic because at the warehouse I just keep doing these exact things, right? Like I was just saying, freezing with my arms up by the forklift, copying the beeping sounds and the hand signals, or moving those little spark plug boxes in strange little patterns on the floor even when everyone is yelling for me to stop. 

If I was in control, wouldn't I just... stop? I mean, think about it.
